tier_reason: fastapprox/tests/testfastexp.c and tests/testmacros.h only assert accuracy against expf (average relative error below 1e-4f for fastexp and vfastexp, below 2e-2f for fasterexp and vfasterexp over 100000 drand48 inputs) and time the approximation alone (1e8 calls on a volatile 1.0f via gettimeofday); libm is never timed and no results file or speed ratio exists in the repo, so there are no speed numbers against the baseline. A search found no reachable first-party or third-party speed figure either.
notes: Record is accurate: the accuracy bounds in claimed_speedup appear in the test file, the timing macro times only the approximation on a constant input, and metadata checks out (13 stars, fork of etheory/fastapprox, no licence detected on the page but BSD-3-Clause text in fastapprox/COPYING, last commit 2017-03-01 'Etheory patch gcc narrowing fix + MSVC support', romeric/fastapprox 222 stars, Rust crate fastapprox 94,746 downloads). Shortcoming to record: no speed measurement against libm anywhere (tier D, speed versus current glibc is hardware-dependent and unmeasured), abandoned since 2017; kept as a widely ported approximation library rather than rejected.

tier_reason: docs/reports/gcc_intel_i5_13600/itoa.html carries the yy and fmtlib rows exactly as claimed (random length average cycles: u32 20.69 vs 40.37, u64 33.55 vs 56.88, i32 21.33 vs 53.62, i64 33.47 vs 65.65) with compiler GCC 13.2.0 and CPU i5-13600KF stated; the benchmark code (src/itoa/itoa_fmtlib.cpp calling fmt::format_to(buf, FMT_COMPILE("{}"), val), the yy implementation and run_itoa) and the build flags (CMakeLists.txt defaults to Release, adds -falign-functions=64 for GCC) are public, so it is reproducible.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Random-length itoa, average CPU cycles per call, GCC 13.2.0 on Intel i5-13600KF: yy 20.69 vs fmtlib 40.37 for u32 (1.95x, derived from page data), 33.55 vs 56.88 for u64 (1.70x, derived from page data), 21.33 vs 53.62 for i32 (2.51x, derived from page data), 33.47 vs 65.65 for i64 (1.96x, derived from page data). Same direction on Clang 18.1.3 (u64 34.10 vs 53.93), MSVC 1940 (u64 42.50 vs 71.73) and Apple M1 Pro with Apple Clang 15.0.0 (u64 26.88 vs 43.44); the null no-op group is about 4 cycles (5.66 in the GCC u32 chart, 3.0 on the M1).
corrections.compiler_and_flags: GCC 13.2.0 (other reports: Clang 18.1.3, MSVC 1940, Apple Clang 15.0.0); CMake Release build (CMAKE_BUILD_TYPE defaults to Release in CMakeLists.txt, so CMake's default -O3 -DNDEBUG for GCC and Clang and /O2 for MSVC; C11 and C++17), GCC gets -falign-functions=64 and Clang -mllvm -align-all-functions=7; the ARCH_NATIVE option (-march=native) defaults to OFF and the report does not say whether it was used
corrections.caveats: (1) The repo times fmt's compile-time format_to path (src/itoa/itoa_fmtlib.cpp; vendor/fmt submodule pinned at commit 0379bf3, version not checked), not std::to_chars, fmt::format_int or sprintf; sprintf is registered only as the correctness oracle. (2) The benchmark and the yy function have the same author, but the code, compiler versions and CPU model are public. (3) Cycle counts include loop overhead (null group about 4 cycles, 5.66 in the GCC u32 chart); the reported CPU frequency (5090 MHz) suggests turbo boost was on although the README advises turning it off. (4) The interactive reports are served from github.io, which is not reachable here, so the numbers were read from the report HTML committed under docs/reports. (5) yy is not the fastest in the report: yy_largelut, an and jeaiii beat it in several columns (u64 random on GCC: yy_largelut 22.02, an 29.40, jeaiii 33.32, yy 33.55 cycles). (6) Independent corroboration against the listed baselines, from the raw google/benchmark rows of https://raw.githubusercontent.com/simditoa/benchmarks/HEAD/RESULTS.md (repo https://github.com/simditoa/benchmarks, 0 stars, written by a rival integer-formatting project; benchmarks/yy_itoa.cpp calls itoa_i64_yy and benchmarks/fmtlib_fmt.cpp calls fmt::format_int; Intel Xeon Platinum 8481C c3-standard-8 VM, CMake Release with -mavx512* flags, compiler version and C++ standard library not printed): geometric mean of the _mean ints/s rows over {UNIFORM_POS, LOG_HEAVY, FIXED 12, 16, 19} is 136.1M for itoa_i64_yy, 62.4M for std::to_chars (2.18x, derived from page data) and 83.2M for fmt::format_int (1.64x, derived from page data); the _max rows give 136.3M, 62.5M and 83.4M. yy beats std::to_chars in every measured shape (1.25x at 4 digits up to 2.97x on uniform signed 64-bit values) but loses to fmt::format_int on short numbers (1 digit: 522.4M vs 983.9M ints/s; 4 digits: 399.0M vs 454.1M, mean rows). That file's LLM-written summary scoreboard lists yy_itoa at 103M against std_to_chars 105M and puts the FIXED:1 values in its UNIFORM_POS column, which contradicts its own raw rows, so only the raw rows were used. Because of the unstated compiler that corroboration is tier C by itself.

notes: Record checks out against all four committed reports, the fmtlib wrapper source, the vendor/fmt pin and the repo metadata (MIT, 75 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-12-05, active). Small fixes: the simditoa corroboration figures were taken from the _max aggregate rows (mean rows differ by under 0.3 percent, ratios unchanged), and the null group is up to 5.66 cycles. Shortcomings to record: baseline is fmt's FMT_COMPILE format_to rather than std::to_chars (std::to_chars only in a rival's third-party run with unstated toolchain), first-party benchmark, turbo apparently on, yy beaten by yy_largelut, an and jeaiii in several columns and by fmt::format_int on 1-4 digit numbers.
